articles.title: Daily and Seasonal Activity Patterns of the Endemic Balkan Snow Vole (Dinaromys bogdanovi) Within a Sympatric Small Mammal Community
paragraphs: Species found only in small geographic areas contribute to regional biodiversity, but gaps in basic knowledge about their ecology can make conservation planning difficult. Over three years, we used motion-activated cameras to study the daily and seasonal activity of the Balkan snow vole, a small endemic mammal restricted to the western Balkans, and other small mammals living in the same habitat in Biokovo Nature Park, Croatia. The Balkan snow vole remained active throughout the year, predominantly at night, with low levels of daytime activity in spring, autumn, and winter. Its activity patterns varied among seasons and differed from those of other small mammals in spring, autumn, and winter. In summer, activity was concentrated at night, and we detected no significant differences between the vole and the other groups studied. The study also provides new information on the activity of the poorly known Dinaric population of the garden dormouse. Our findings demonstrate the value of long-term camera monitoring for studying small mammals that are otherwise difficult to observe. This information can help guide wildlife surveys, provide a baseline for detecting future changes in activity, and inform conservation planning for regional biodiversity.

Understanding the temporal ecology of endemic species is important for conservation planning in biodiversity hotspots during global climate change and habitat alteration. We used three years of camera-trap monitoring across two deployment periods to quantify daily and seasonal activity patterns of the endemic Balkan snow vole (Dinaromys bogdanovi) and sympatric terrestrial small mammals in Biokovo Nature Park, Croatia, within the Western Balkan glacial refugia. Dinaromys bogdanovi was predominantly nocturnal, with minor but consistent diurnal activity, and shifted from multimodal nocturnal activity in spring, summer and autumn to a unimodal winter peak. Temporal niche differentiation occurred between D. bogdanovi and the sympatric small mammals during some seasons. These differences were associated with nocturnal peak timing and the greater diurnal activity of D. bogdanovi. In summer, the detected taxa showed greater overlap in predominantly nocturnal activity, consistent with a possible influence of thermal conditions on surface activity, although temperature was not measured. We also provide quantitative activity data for the geographically isolated Dinaric population of Eliomys quercinus. This study demonstrates the value of long-term camera trapping for monitoring cryptic small mammals and provides a baseline for evaluating future changes in activity, habitat use and community interactions, supporting conservation planning for endemic species facing climate change and anthropogenic pressures.

articles.title: Towards Intelligent Membrane Systems: A Critical Analysis of Digital Twin–ML Integration for Real–Time Process Optimization, Fouling Management, and Autonomous Design
paragraphs: Membrane separation is central to potable water production, wastewater reclamation, desalination, gas separation, and decarbonization, yet its economics remain constrained by fouling and by a gap between process data and timely operating decisions. Digital twins (DTs) offer live, bidirectionally coupled virtual representations of physical assets, while machine learning (ML) extracts predictive and prescriptive insights from operational data. Together, they are promising computational approaches for membrane systems. However, their applications have largely evolved independently across fouling prediction, DT development, and ML-based materials discovery. This review argues that these are converging strands of a single trajectory toward self-sensing, self-predicting, and eventually self-designing membrane systems, and that treating them separately obscures key interdependencies. The contributions are threefold. First, applying the digital model/digital shadow/digital twin taxonomy, it shows that most published membrane DTs are digital shadows (DSs). Second, it proposes a five-level autonomy framework, inspired by vehicle automation taxonomies, providing a unified scale for comparing applications ranging from LSTM-based fouling forecasting and reinforcement learning dosing control to autonomous materials laboratories. Third, it integrates autonomous materials design, including self-driving laboratories, inverse design, generative models, and Bayesian search, into the upper levels of this ladder. Evidence is synthesized across reverse osmosis, nanofiltration, ultrafiltration, microfiltration, membrane bioreactors, membrane distillation, and gas separation membranes, with emphasis on critically assessing model performance and generalizability. The study concludes with a roadmap for overcoming data limitations, poor interpretability, interoperability gaps, cybersecurity risks, techno-economic barriers, and regulatory trust deficits that block autonomous membrane systems.

articles.title: Catchment structure and functioning mediates beaver activity in contrasting lowland agricultural landscapes
paragraphs: The reintroduction of beavers in Germany and across Europe has revived interest in their function as ecosystem engineers and their associated impacts on landscapes, hydrological regimes, and water quality. Despite mounting evidence of effects on the hydrology and water quality of rivers, beaver distribution and the links to landscape heterogeneity are still poorly understood. In this study, an extensive intercomparison of two topographically contrasting lowland agricultural catchments was conducted—the Sophienfliess (SOFL) and the Demnitzer Mill Creek (DMC), both in Eastern Brandenburg, Germany. The goal of this study was to assess how catchment structure and functioning mediate beaver activity in terms of distribution and dam density, and how this in turn affects water and nutrient fluxes. A survey of beaver dams in terms of dam location, density, and attributes in both catchments revealed significant differences in the evolution of beaver habitat over time, the number of dams present, and their effects on water flow and nutrient cycling. Most notably, in the lower SOFL catchment, dam density has increased steadily over the last decade and was almost 10 times higher compared to the DMC catchment. In contrast, the recent multi‐year drought in Eastern Germany, as well as differential catchment functioning, has led to reduced beaver activity in the DMC catchment, despite recent wetland rehabilitation efforts. Furthermore, physical differences in dam structure and size could be linked to landscape settings (i.e., valley gradient), surface‐groundwater connectivity, and channel characteristics (straightened vs. meandering). In SOFL, a beaver dam cascade system in the lower catchment propagated significant denitrification, reduction in dissolved organic carbon, and phosphorus concentrations. In contrast, the spatial dynamics of nutrient fluxes in the DMC revealed more localized mobilization processes and strong responses of solutes to hydrological connectivity, which could not be solely linked to beaver activity. Overall, the study showed that catchment structure, hydrological conditions, and stream channel characteristics influence how and where beaver dams are established, and how they in turn influence the physical, chemical, and biological characteristics of surface waters.

articles.title: Outdoor Environmental Risk Factors for Paediatric Ragweed Sensitisation: A Formal Model Comparison

PM10 and categorical pollen exposure were statistically equivalent predictors of ragweed sensitisation, consistent with their strong area-level correlation; NO2 provided no additional information; indoor exposures added no independent risk.Children with more green space within 5 km of home and children living in rural locations were less often sensitised; whether broadleaved forest cover explains the rural association could not be determined.

What are the implications of the main findings? When two environmental exposures are highly correlated, comparing models by an information criterion shows whether the data can tell them apart at all, which guards against attributing sensitisation risk to one exposure when the two cannot be statistically distinguished.The association between surrounding green space and lower paediatric ragweed sensitisation is hypothesis-generating; confirmation in longitudinal studies would be needed before drawing implications for urban greening as a preventive strategy.

The association between surrounding green space and lower paediatric ragweed sensitisation is hypothesis-generating; confirmation in longitudinal studies would be needed before drawing implications for urban greening as a preventive strategy.

Background/Objectives: Ragweed (Ambrosia artemisiifolia) is a major aeroallergen in Central and Eastern Europe. Croatian children in regions with twofold difference in pollen exposure show near-identical sensitisation prevalence (the “Zagreb paradox”), and an earlier analysis found regional pollen and rural residence to be the only associated environmental factors. We re-examined whether air pollution, surrounding landscape and indoor environment contribute to it. Methods: This cross-sectional analysis used 3520 of the 4016 children recruited to the EU FP7 ATOPICA study, who had their complete data re-analysed within the EU Horizon Europe EDIAQI project. Sensitisation was defined as a skin prick test wheal of at least 2 mm. Environmental predictors (particulate matter, PM10; nitrogen dioxide, NO2; regional pollen; CORINE land cover within 5 km; rural residence; and indoor exposures) were compared using the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) in logistic regression models, which were adjusted for age and parental atopy. Results: Sensitisation prevalence was 10.8%. PM10 and categorical pollen area fitted the data equally well (ΔAIC 1.7): both describe the same inland-coastal contrast and cannot be distinguished with area-level data. NO2 added nothing to either. Of the 16 landscape variables, only transitional woodland-shrub remained associated with sensitisation after Bonferroni correction (adjusted odds ratio, aOR 0.93 [95% confidence interval, CI 0.90–0.97]); total green area was nominally associated (aOR 0.92 [95% CI 0.87–0.98]; p = 0.009). articles.title: ACMNet: An attention-convolution mixed neural network for semantic segmentation of high-resolution remote sensing images
paragraphs: Semantic segmentation of remote sensing imagery, which is widely used in land cover classification, urban planning, and environmental monitoring, has become a research hotspot in the fields of remote sensing and computer vision. As its applications continue to expand, improving the segmentation accuracy and generalization have become pressing challenges. However, most existing semantic segmentation models rely solely on either attention mechanisms or convolutional neural networks (CNNs), thus leaving room for performance improvement. In this study, we propose ACMNet (Attention-Convolution Mixed Network), which adopts a hybrid attention-convolution architecture. The decoder of ACMNet employs an innovative mixed design, where two branches are used to extract and integrate different types of contextual information and achieve hierarchical aggregation of contextual features, thereby enhancing its performance. To evaluate the performance of ACMNet, we conducted ablation experiments and comparative experiments on the Potsdam, Vaihingen, and WHU Building datasets. The results show that ACMNet achieved the best overall performance across all three datasets, with mF1 scores of 91.79%, 88.70%, and 96.56% on the Potsdam, Vaihingen, and WHU Building datasets, respectively. These findings indicate that ACMNet delivers superior performance in the semantic segmentation of high-resolution remote sensing images in urban areas, which provides valuable support for diverse tasks related to fine-grained urban management and dynamic monitoring.

articles.title: Air pollution is associated with a distinct pathogen spectrum in community-acquired pneumonia: a prospective multicentre cohort study
paragraphs: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) is the leading cause of death due to infection worldwide, with its incidence and disease course influenced by air pollution exposure. Little is known about how air pollution influences microbiological findings in patients with CAP.

Patients were recruited from a prospective, multicentre study of CAP (CAPNETZ). Air pollution data were collected at the city level considering data up to one month before inclusion. Associations with sputum pathogen detection and cell counts were tested using generalised linear mixed-effects logistic regression models adjusting for clinical confounders, centre-level heterogeneity and meteorological data. Internal validation was performed using an Ensemble Feature Selection (EFS) approach.

Among 4,446 eligible patients with available sputum samples, a potential pathogen was detected in 1,581 patients, while complete sputum-cell-count data were available for 4,014 patients. Detection of Streptococcus pneumoniae was associated with previous higher exposure to sulphur dioxide (SO2) (OR 1.75, p = 0.008) and carbon monoxide (CO) (OR 1.57, p = 0.02). Escherichia coli was more frequently detected in patients who were exposed to elevated levels of nitrogen dioxide (NO2) (OR 2.75, p = 0.004) and higher temperature (OR 1.51, p = 0.03), whereas increased fine particulate matter (PM2.5) exposure (OR 0.37, p = 0.001) was linked to reduced detection. Furthermore, SO2 exposure influenced the likelihood of obtaining a diagnostically relevant sputum culture and was associated with higher odds of detecting a high leucocyte count (OR 1.18, p = 0.02). Results were largely corroborated by EFS, particularly for S. pneumoniae and E. coli detection.

Exposure to air pollution was associated with a distinct pathogen spectrum in patients with CAP. These findings may have implications for the interpretation of microbiological data in an epidemiological and clinical context and highlight the importance of considering air pollution exposure as a confounding factor. Further validation in cohorts with high-quality environmental, microbiological and antimicrobial resistance data is needed.

articles.title: Elephant Presence Shapes Butterfly Communities in an East African Coastal Forest
paragraphs: Habitat disturbances shape the diversity and composition of plant and animal species. It is important to distinguish between natural disturbances caused by megaherbivores and anthropogenic disturbances caused by human activity, as different disturbance regimes differently affect biodiversity. In this study, we analyse butterfly diversity and community structure in three forest areas with different habitat disturbances in the Arabuko Sokoke dry coastal forest of south‐eastern Kenya. We assessed butterfly diversity with bait‐traps in primary forest with and without elephants, and in secondary forest characterised by previous human use and where elephants are currently present. In total, we activated 24 traps, eight traps per forest type. We found differences in the butterfly diversity and community structure depending on forest type and disturbance regime. The rather dense primary forest harboured a considerably higher proportion of dark‐coloured forest butterfly species than the secondary forest, particularly in areas with elephant disturbance. The secondary forest has higher butterfly species richness than the primary forest due to the occurrence of savannah species. Correspondence analyses clearly separated the three forest types with respect to community composition. Species occurring also in anthropogenic habitats were significantly more abundant in the secondary forest than in the two primary forest types. Our findings underline that forest type and disturbance regime shape butterfly diversity and community structure. Our study underlines that the effects of natural disturbances and human‐induced disturbances on butterfly diversity differ fundamentally. Natural disturbances such as by elephant activities seem to promote typical forest butterflies.

articles.title: AVISNet: An edge-computing model for acoustic identification of species from the Doñana bird community
paragraphs: The global decline in biodiversity calls for scalable and efficient species monitoring. Birds, as sensitive ecological indicators with rich vocal activity, are particularly well suited for passive acoustic monitoring (PAM), which enables extensive, non-invasive data collection. Yet the large volumes of audio generated by PAM require automated and efficient processing pipelines to extract meaningful biological information in real time. To address this challenge, we integrated automated acoustic species identification directly into embedded devices (i.e., at the edge), enabling autonomous on-site data processing without reliance on cloud-based computation. Our methodology emphasizes model efficiency and leverages lightweight pre-trained architectures (e.g., MobileNet), alongside advanced learning strategies such as knowledge distillation and few-shot learning to overcome data scarcity for under-represented species. This methodology was applied as a case study to acoustic identification of bird species native to Doñana National Park, Spain. We assessed the performance and efficiency of our models at three levels of acoustic data: focal segments, focal recordings, and soundscape recordings. On focal recordings, our models achieve up to 0.70 F1-score in species identification task. At the soundscape level, we evaluated performance using three real-world soundscape datasets, measuring accuracy metrics at both the vocalization and dataset levels. Overall, our results show that these networks achieve functional species recognition performance while substantially reducing inference latency and energy requirements relative to BirdNET, thus enabling on-device deployment on low-power units. articles.title: Review on modelling of thermoset and thermoplastic composites: constitutive equations, processing modelling and multiphysics modelling
paragraphs: Fibre-reinforced composites have emerged as pivotal materials in advanced structural applications across aerospace, automotive, marine, and renewable energy sectors, due to their superior specific strength, stiffness, toughness, recyclability, and rapid manufacturing potential. Composites manufacturing involves complex multiscale, multiphysics phenomena, including melting, crystallisation, flow, fibre orientation, and residual stress generation that significantly influence the final component quality and performance. Process modelling has become an indispensable tool to address these challenges, enabling the prediction of manufacturing-induced defects, residual stresses and dimensional distortion, and reduction of reliance on physical trials. This review examines current process modelling approaches for thermoset and thermoplastic fibrereinforced composites, with emphasis on the constitutive equations, process simulation methodologies and multiscale modelling frameworks used to predict process-induced phenomena. Particular attention is given to predictive frameworks for temperature evolution, crystallinity development, fibre orientation, residual stress generation, and process-induced distortion. Modelling approaches ranging from conventional finite element methods and molecular dynamics to meshless methods and machine-learning-based techniques are critically reviewed and compared with respect to their capabilities, limitations and application domains. Emphasis is given to the integration of process simulation with experimental monitoring and to the transfer of process-induced material states and defects to structural-level performance models. Key challenges that have been identified include uncertainty quantification, computational efficiency, model transferability, and the limited integration of physics-based and data-driven approaches. Future developments are expected to focus on validated multiscale process-structure-performance frameworks, uncertainty quantification, hybrid physics-informed data-driven modelling, and digital-twin-assisted process monitoring to enhance predictive reliability and accelerate the industrial adoption of composite process modelling and simulation.

articles.title: Microclimatic regulation effects of landscape elements on university campus in a temperate monsoon climate zone: A case study during extreme summer heat
paragraphs: Although temperate monsoon climate regions are traditionally known for their harsh winter climates, the combined effects of rapid urbanization and global climate change have significantly intensified summer urban heat island effects in these areas, making them a neglected yet increasingly severe challenge in high-latitude urban climate adaptation planning. This study takes a typical campus in Shenyang, a temperate monsoon climate region in Northeast China, as the experimental subject. It quantitatively dissects the non-linear statistical associations and regulatory mechanisms of biotic and abiotic landscape elements and their spatial configurations on microclimate parameters and human thermal comfort (Physiologically Equivalent Temperature, PET) by combining microclimate field observations with validated ENVI-met numerical simulations. Field measurement results show that the vertical structural characteristics of vegetation dominate cooling efficiency: evergreen trees and shrubs, with their dense radiation-blocking structures, exhibit optimal regulatory potential, with mean Physiological Equivalent Temperature (ΔPET) values reaching 10.6°C and 10.4°C, respectively, significantly outperforming deciduous trees (8.1°C). In contrast, abiotic elements play an auxiliary role, with dynamic water bodies and enclosed pavilions providing PET improvement values of 3.1°C and 2.9°C, respectively, while paving materials have limited direct regulatory capacity (< 2.0°C). Simulation optimization further reveals a significant “blue-green synergy” effect: the composite configuration of high-canopy evergreen trees and large-area dynamic water bodies forms the optimal spatial solution, reducing daily average PET to 48.7°C, a decrease of 7.3°C compared to the vegetation-free baseline scenario. Addressing the unique “humid-heat” challenge that distinguishes temperate monsoon climates from arid or semi-arid regions where summer thermal stress is often attributed solely to high temperatures, this study goes beyond merely documenting cooling effects to elucidate the “structural-thermal decoupling” mechanism in temperate monsoon climates. It challenges the conventional “deciduous-first” design paradigm by quantifying the superior radiative-blocking efficiency of evergreen species during extreme heatwaves, providing a physically-grounded framework for campus microclimate resilience.

articles.title: Substantial Neotropical bat diversity likely remains undescribed and vulnerable to extinction
paragraphs: Numerous undescribed species face extinction before formal scientific recognition. Despite research advances, the exceptional bat diversity of the Neotropics remains overlooked, with accelerating habitat loss threatening unrecognized lineages with silent extinction, requiring urgent conservation prioritization. Here, we integrate molecular species delimitation, phylogenetic inference, ecological niche modelling, and spatial conservation analyses to identify 95 Neotropical bat lineages that may represent undescribed species within 45 complexes, revealing that at least one-fifth of the recognized taxa may harbor hidden diversity spanning the entire evolutionary spectrum. This overlooked diversity faces a countdown to extinction: 62% of complexes face imminent habitat loss, and most are projected to lose over 50% of their suitable habitat by 2070. At current description rates, formally recognizing this diversity would take decades, a timeframe these putative species cannot afford. We develop a Hidden Species Richness (HSR) Index that pinpoints ten hidden diversity hotspots where undescribed richness coincides with significant human threats and extreme climate vulnerability. These hotspots highlight regions where research efforts are most needed, transforming crises into priorities. This race against extinction requires immediate taxonomic attention to document this biodiversity before it vanishes.

Many Neotropical bat species may be disappearing before scientists can even describe them. The study identified 95 candidate lineages across 45 complexes and found many overlap with areas of habitat loss, indicating urgent conservation needs.

articles.title: Phenological divergence between flowering plants and flower-visiting Lepidoptera under climate change across Europe
paragraphs: Climate change is altering life-cycle timing and may disrupt coordinated interactions between flowering plants and flower-visiting insects. Using Global Biodiversity Information Facility observation records from Europe between 2000 and 2024, we compiled a continental-scale phenological dataset covering flowering periods of 707 angiosperm species and adult activity periods of 620 Lepidoptera species. We extracted the 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles and activity-window width and used linear mixed-effects models to analyse spatio-temporal trends. The results showed that plant phenology advanced significantly, with the 10th and 50th percentiles shifting earlier by −0.597 and −0.507 d yr⁻¹, respectively, whereas the 90th percentile showed no significant change; flowering-window width increased by 0.361 d yr⁻¹. By contrast, Lepidoptera phenology advanced evenly across the season, with the 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles shifting by −0.137, −0.153 and −0.155 d yr⁻¹, respectively, while activity-window width showed no significant change. Because flowering plants advanced faster than Lepidoptera in the early and middle season, plant–insect phenological overlap declined at 0.340 d yr⁻¹, indicating increasing mismatch across Europe. Further analyses identified temperature as the dominant driver of phenological advance in both groups, but flowering plants and Lepidoptera differed in their responses to other climatic factors. These results suggest that climate change is weakening phenological synchrony between flowering plants and flower-visiting Lepidoptera, with potential consequences for pollination and ecosystem functioning.

articles.title: Soil amendments reshape alpine meadow microbial communities across degradation gradients by modulating nutrient availability
paragraphs: Climate change and overgrazing have led to the continued degradation of alpine meadows on the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau, thereby severely impairing the ecosystem services provided by these grasslands. Soil amendments are an important strategy for restoring degraded grasslands; however, the regulatory effects of different amendment measures across varying degradation gradients and the underlying microbial response mechanisms remain unclear. This study systematically investigated the effects of three soil amendments (humic acid, superabsorbent polymer, and Bacillus subtilis) on soil physicochemical properties and microbial community structure in mildly, moderately, and severely degraded alpine meadows. The results indicated that the regulatory effects of soil amendments are significantly dependent on the degradation gradient: In the severe degradation stage, amendments significantly increased available nutrients, lowered pH, and alleviated alkalization, whereas their regulatory effects were limited in the mild degradation stage. Amendments selectively altered the abundance of microbial groups involved in organic matter degradation, nitrogen cycling, and stress-tolerant symbiosis. Humic acid demonstrated the optimal regulatory effect in the mild degradation stage, whereas superabsorbent polymers and Bacillus subtilis were more suitable for restoration in the moderate and severe degradation stages. Redundancy analysis indicated that bacterial communities were primarily subject to deterministic selection by soil pH, available potassium, and organic matter gradients, with the intensity of environmental selection increasing with increasing degradation severity; fungal communities exhibited significant environmental responses only in the moderate degradation stage, while stochastic processes dominated community assembly in the mild and severe degradation stages. In summary, alpine meadows at various stages of degradation require differentiated remediation strategies. Precise, stage-specific remediation tailored to degradation severity can facilitate synergistic restoration of the soil–microbial system, providing a theoretical basis and practical guidance for restoring degraded alpine meadows on the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau.

articles.title: Spatiotemporal monitoring of water quality degradation and trophic state in a severely polluted tropical urban lake in Southern India
paragraphs: Bellandur Lake in Bangalore, India represents one of the most severely polluted urban water bodies in South Asia, necessitating systematic monitoring for environmental management. This study employed Sentinel-2 Multispectral Instrument imagery to assess spatiotemporal variations in water quality parameters from January 2023 to December 2025. Six water quality indicators were derived using established remote sensing algorithms: chlorophyll-a (estimated using the Normalised Difference Chlorophyll Index as the primary method), turbidity, total suspended solids, coloured dissolved organic matter, Secchi depth, and floating algae index. A total of 100 Sentinel-2 images were processed using Google Earth Engine, yielding 93 valid observations across 28 months after excluding monsoon periods affected by cloud cover and confining analysis to complete years 2023–2025. Results indicated severely degraded conditions with mean NDCI-based chlorophyll-a of 71.31 µg/L (median 70.24 µg/L), consistently classifying the lake as hypereutrophic. Mann–Kendall trend analysis revealed statistically significant increasing trends in chlorophyll-a (τ = 0.144, p = 0.041) and floating algae index (τ = 0.419, p < 0.001), with concurrent significant decreasing trends in turbidity (p < 0.001) and total suspended solids (p = 0.001). Pixel-wise FDR-corrected trend analysis identified 33.7% of the lake area exhibiting significant increasing chlorophyll-a trends. The lake consistently exceeded Central Pollution Control Board standards, with 100% of observations surpassing permissible total suspended solids limits and 98.9% of observations classified as hypereutrophic. These findings are interpreted as indicative of relative spatial and temporal patterns given the absence of site-specific in situ calibration; however, they provide valuable baseline information for management interventions and demonstrate the utility of satellite remote sensing for monitoring polluted urban water bodies.
The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s11356-026-38316-4.

articles.title: Environmental health determinants among seasonal migrants in China: a multi-dimensional analysis
paragraphs: To conduct a systematic review of the evidence regarding the impact of environmental health factors, such as air pollution, thermal stress, water and soil pollution, agricultural instability, and occupational hazards, on seasonal migration in China.

A systematic review of PubMed, Web of Science, CNKI, Scopus, and Google Scholar (2001–2025) was conducted to identify peer-reviewed articles and institutional reports on environmental exposure, health, and migration outcomes in the Chinese mainland’s populations.

Outmigration trends were found to be associated with each of the four aspects of air pollution, heat stress, water contamination, and agricultural instability during the winter, and, in addition to the above, water and soil contamination, in the summer. The effects were found to be strongest among rural poor and older individuals. At urban destinations, migrants were also at risk of occupational hazards due to silica dust and chemicals.

The environment exerts a multidimensional, seasonal influence on internal migration in China. There is a need for coordinated environmental health governance to minimize migrant exposure and promote health equity in this population.

articles.title: Engineering the plant holobiont for enhanced abiotic stress resilience: current insights and future directions
paragraphs: Climate change has intensified abiotic stresses such as drought, heat, and salinity, posing major threats to agricultural productivity and global food security. Conventional strategies to improve crop tolerance often face limitations in efficiency, sustainability, and environmental adaptability, underscoring the need for innovative approaches. This review focuses on the plant holobiont, which views plants and their associated microbiomes as an integrated functional unit in governing stress adaptation. Abiotic stress can disrupt plant-associated microbial communities, leading to dysbiosis and reduced holobiont resilience. Beneficial microorganisms, including plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria, endophytes, and arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, can enhance stress tolerance by improving nutrient acquisition, regulating phytohormone signaling, strengthening antioxidant defenses, maintaining osmotic balance, and modulating stress-responsive gene expression. Emerging evidence suggests that these interactions contribute to the establishment of holobiont stress adaptation through biochemical signaling, microenvironmental modification, and epigenetic regulation, enabling plants to respond more effectively to recurrent stress. Advances in microbiome engineering, particularly through the development of synthetic microbial communities (SynComs), offer promising opportunities to restore microbial functions and enhance crop resilience under changing climatic conditions. The integration of multi-omics technologies, artificial intelligence, and precision agriculture is expected to accelerate the development of microbiome-based solutions for sustainable crop production. Collectively, microbiome engineering represents a promising, environmentally sustainable strategy to enhance the holobiont’s adaptive resilience and improve long-term plant performance under abiotic stress.

articles.title: Using Artificial Intelligence to Optimize Ecological Restoration for Climate and Biodiversity
paragraphs: The restoration of degraded ecosystems is critical for mitigating climate change and reversing biodiversity loss. Depending on the primary objective—such as maximizing carbon sequestration or protecting threatened species—and within the boundaries of budget limitations, different spatial priorities have been identified at global and regional scales. Funding mechanisms to support such work comprise public sources, philanthropy, and the private sector, including the sale of carbon and biodiversity credits. However, effectively exploring trade‐offs among restoration objectives and estimating the price of biodiversity and carbon credits to design financially viable projects remains scientifically challenging. Here we harness the power of artificial intelligence implemented in the software CAPTAIN to identify spatial priorities for ecological restoration that maximize multiple objectives at once and to allow a robust evaluation of biodiversity and climate outcomes. We find through a series of simulations that even low‐to‐moderate consideration of biodiversity in the design of restoration projects leads to the selection of restored areas that disproportionately improve the conservation of threatened species, while the carbon captured is only slightly reduced. We propose the bundling of biodiversity and carbon credits to support restoration efforts even in areas previously excluded for economic reasons. Applying our methodology to plant diversity in the Atlantic Forest of eastern South America, one of the most biodiverse and threatened ecosystems globally, we demonstrate its potential to guide restoration and to quantify trade‐offs between multiple optimization scenarios. Our study provides a robust, scalable method to maximize the joint benefits of ecological restoration for climate and nature.

articles.title: Associations between air pollution, accelerated biological aging, and oral inflammatory diseases: evidence from the UK Biobank cohort
paragraphs: The relationships between air pollution exposure and incident risk of oral inflammatory diseases (OIDs) and roles of accelerated biological aging remain unclear.

In 348,247 adults from the UK Biobank, the individual levels of air pollutants, including particulate matter (PM) (PM2.5, PM10, PM2.5–10, and PM2.5 absorbance), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), nitric oxides (NOx), and air pollution score (multiple air pollutants exposure), were estimated. The associations between air pollution exposure and incident risk of OIDs were assessed. The mediation roles of the Klemera–Doubal method biological age (KDM-BA) acceleration and the phenotypic age (PhenoAge) acceleration were evaluated.

During the median follow-up of 16.49 years, a total of 3,967 incident OIDs were documented. Each one standard deviation increment in PM2.5, PM10, PM2.5–10, PM2.5 absorbance, NO2, NOx, and air pollution score was significantly associated with 8%, 4%, 3%, 5%, 10%, 8%, and 8% increments in incident risk of OIDs, respectively (all p < 0.05). All air pollutants except PM2.5–10 were significantly and positively associated with KDM-BA acceleration, and all air pollutants were significantly and positively associated with PhenoAge acceleration (all p < 0.05). KDM-BA acceleration mediated the associations between all air pollution (except PM2.5–10) and incident risk of OIDs, with mediation proportion ranging from 1.21 to 5.42%. PhenoAge acceleration mediated the associations between all air pollutants and incident risk of OIDs, with mediation proportion ranging from 8.52 to 16.65%.
Air pollution may contribute to increased incident risk of OIDs, and premature aging may play an important role in the pathogenic process.

articles.title: Improving Micro– and Macro–Algae Speciation Mapping for Management: A Field‐Validated Sentinel‐2 and Sentinel‐3 Intercomparison in the Indian River Lagoon
paragraphs: In recent years, the health of the Indian River Lagoon (IRL) on Florida's east coast has fluctuated due to recurring harmful algal blooms (HABs). These events typically involve cyanobacteria, dinoflagellates, or A. lagunensis (brown tide) causing water‐quality degradation and seagrass decline. The IRL is prone to HAB formation, and they have been observed more commonly in recent years. Although HABs can be non‐toxic, they can threaten critical primary producers like seagrass and destabilize sediments. Due to their impact, it is critical to improve methods of water quality and algal bloom monitoring. To do this, we apply a multi‐image varimax‐rotated principal component analysis (VPCA) to images from a harmonized Sentinel‐2 A/B multispectral imager (MSI) data set spanning three years (2020–2022). Field collected hyperspectral data and a coincident Sentinel‐3 A/B OLCI image is used to further validate the multi‐image VPCA. The VPCA method employs visible derivative water surface reflectance and unmixes the spectral signal to identify orthogonal components related to divisions of algae, suspended sediments, and seagrass. This advances water quality monitoring by improving unmixing and identification of optical components over time. This identification is supported by high correlation to a spectral library, field observation, published observations, and validation across sensors of varying resolutions. Through this research we find confident identification and mapping of in‐water components related to cyanobacterial (component 1 r 2 = 0.865) and dinoflagellate blooms (component 4 and 5 r 2 = 0.986 and r 2 = 0.978), and seagrass beds (component 3 r 2 = 0.916) with 10 m spatial resolution through time improving water quality monitoring and root cause identification.

The Indian River Lagoon (IRL) in Florida has experienced fluctuating water quality in recent years due to harmful algae blooms (HABs). These blooms are often caused by species of algae like cyanobacteria, brown tide, and dinoflagellates. An algae bloom can grow so dense that it can block sunlight from other species like seagrass and cause other harmful effects to the ecosystem. Parts of the IRL have high nutrients caused by sewage pollution that enable HABs to occur. Due to HABs becoming more common, a better technique for monitoring water quality and algae extent is necessary to assist environmental agencies and decision makers. To improve these monitoring systems, we use a multi‐image remote sensing method (VPCA) to process 10 m spatial resolution Sentinel‐2 A/B images over a 3‐year period. By doing this we can unmix spectrally complex reflectance data, identify micro‐ and macro‐algae, and develop time‐series maps of water constituents.

articles.title: Air pollution exposure during urban running in Frankfurt, Germany: a randomized crossover comparison of particulate matter levels on park, roadside, and residential routes across morning and early afternoon hours
paragraphs: In urban environments, physical activity-induced health effects may be diminished by exposure to air pollution. Typical avoidance strategies, such as running through green spaces or avoiding major roads and rush hours, have not yet been adequately validated. This study quantified particulate matter exposure during running across three adjacent urban microenvironments: a major roadside, a residential area, and an urban park, accounting for diurnal variation.

Mobile measurements of particulate matter with aerodynamic diameters ≤ 10 μm (PM10), ≤ 2.5 μm (PM2.5), and ≤ 1 μm (PM1) as well as local urban background concentrations of PM2.5 and PM10 were collected during 2 km runs (n = 60, pace 8:02–4:31 min/km). Runs on major roads (n = 20), residential streets (n = 20), or in an urban park (n = 20), as well as runs in the morning (n = 30) and in the early afternoon (n = 30), were equally distributed. Differences between routes, incorporating the effects of daytime and meteorological factors, on particulate matter concentrations were analysed using linear mixed-effects models.

The lowest concentrations across PM fractions occurred during early-afternoon runs in the park, whereas the highest exposure to PM10 across all environments was reached during morning runs on the same route. In line with the urban background levels, exposure across all routes was lower during early-afternoon than during morning runs. Humidity, air pressure, wind speed, and temperature were associated with particulate matter exposure during running. A sensitivity analysis using run-level means (n = 60) did not confirm the route or route×daytime effects as statistically significant, indicating that these patterns require confirmation in larger samples.

Running in parks in the early afternoon and avoiding busy morning hours may help reduce fine and submicron particle exposure, particularly during calm, humid, and high-pressure conditions when pollutant dispersion is limited. ​However, park routes did not reduce, and at times increased, coarse-particle (PM10) exposure, especially in the morning. These route- and daytime-related differences were not confirmed in a run-level sensitivity analysis and should therefore be regarded as preliminary.

articles.title: What Is There to Gain? A Systematic Review on Psychosocial Co-Benefits of Climate Policies
paragraphs: Climate change poses major risks to psychosocial health, yet little is known about potential psychosocial co-benefits of climate policies. This systematic review examines (A) psychosocial co-benefits associated with climate policy measures and (B) moderating factors shaping these effects.
Following PRISMA guidelines, k = 21 studies were identified and analysed using a PICOS framework and narrative synthesis.

Climate policies, particularly air pollution control, environmental taxation, and nature-based urban interventions, were associated with improvements in subjective well-being, mental health, and social cohesion. Effects were moderated by environmental improvements and physical health gains, and varied by socioeconomic status, age, and contexts such as schools or rural vs. urban locations. Access to and actual use of interventions emerged as relevant but understudied mechanisms. Some studies indicated trade-offs, including unequal distribution of benefits and unintended social effects.

Overall, climate policies can generate psychosocial co-benefits, but evidence remains heterogeneous and methodologically limited. Future research should strengthen causal inference, standardise outcome measures, and examine long-term and distributional effects.

articles.title: A Comparison of Owl Pellet Analysis and Conventional Trapping: A Review of Central European Cases for the Study of Small Mammal Communities and More Efficient Paleoenvironmental Reconstructions
paragraphs: Due to their rapid reproductive cycles and short generation times, small mammals—particularly rodents and shrews—are widely used as bioindicators in ecological studies. While traditional live trapping provides detailed demographic data for such monitoring, it is labour‐intensive and subject to sampling bias. In contrast, owl pellet analysis presents a non‐invasive and cost‐effective alternative for evaluating small mammal community structure over broad spatial and temporal scales, though potential prey preferences should be considered. This study evaluates the effectiveness of owl pellet analysis in comparison to conventional trapping methods for monitoring small mammal communities. We synthesised data from 26 published studies and additional unpublished field reports, comprising a uniquely robust dataset of 40 systematically processed case studies across seven countries in Central Europe, a biogeographically coherent region. In all cases, trapping and pellet collection were carried out at the same locations and during the same periods, allowing for an exceptional level of methodological consistency. Results reveal that owl pellet analysis detects higher species diversity and provides a more efficient, non‐invasive means of monitoring small mammal assemblages over larger spatial and temporal scales. However, prey preferences and hunting behaviour of owls introduce biases, often overrepresenting abundant prey such as the common vole, Microtus arvalis and underrepresenting species associated with specific habitats or microclimates. These biases have significant implications for biodiversity assessments and paleoenvironmental reconstructions, where accurate community composition is essential. Our findings indicate that while owl pellet analysis is a valuable tool for ecological monitoring, careful consideration of predator selectivity is necessary to accurately interpret the results. Further research into owl hunting ecology is recommended to refine the application of this method in biodiversity studies and paleoecology.
